title: Evaluating the quality and reliability of Kawasaki disease-related content on TikTok and Bilibili: a cross-sectional study
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of the top 100 videos returned by the keyword search for Kawasaki disease on the Chinese versions of TikTok (Douyin) and Bilibili. The study's primary instruments (JAMA, modified DISCERN, PEMAT) are QUALITY scores reported as medians, which alone would not qualify. However, Section 3.7 reports an explicit falsity share with a denominator: 64.58% (31/48) of individual-user videos were identified as containing misinformation, with five named misinformation themes coded against clinical evidence. That is a CONTENT estimate and makes the paper eligible.

estimates.measure_type: % of Kawasaki-disease videos uploaded by individual (lay) users that were judged to contain misinformation
estimates.denominator: 48 Kawasaki-disease videos uploaded by individual (personal) users, out of the 146 included videos from the top 100 search results on each of TikTok and Bilibili
estimates.definition: A video was counted if the researchers' qualitative thematic analysis identified inaccurate/misleading content in it; the five themes were oversimplification of clinical symptoms, incorrect etiological claims, promotion of non-evidence-based home treatments, misinterpretation of diagnostic criteria, and misleading statements regarding immunoglobulin therapy
estimates.misinfo_def: "we conducted a systematic qualitative thematic analysis of videos uploaded by individual users that contained inaccurate information" - no formal definition is offered; accuracy is judged against clinical knowledge of Kawasaki disease and its guidelines
estimates.source_quote: Overall, 64.58% (31/48) of videos uploaded by individual users
estimates.page_loc: Results, Section 3.7 'Qualitative characterization of misinformation themes', p. 9; themes tabulated in Table 5
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two clinician evaluators (Nan Shen, Chang Xu) independently assessed all videos after jointly reviewing the criteria, with a third reviewer (Yongkun Yang) resolving uncertainty; the misinformation themes were derived by qualitative thematic analysis following Colaizzi's seven-step method. Inter-rater ICCs are reported for the scoring instruments (JAMA 0.89, modified DISCERN 0.72, intelligibility 0.85, operability 0.83) but NOT for the binary misinformation judgement itself.
estimates.moderator_quote: We used the keyword "川崎病" (Kawasaki disease) to search the Chinese versions of TikTok and Bilibili (see Figure 1). To minimize bias caused by personalized recommendation algorithms, new accounts were registered and logged in on each platform prior to searching. ... On each platform, the top 100 videos from the search results were retrieved
estimates.notes: Single-disease keyword corpus (topical), rank-truncated to the top 100 hits per platform, hence denom_selection=curated. The 48-video denominator is the subset uploaded by 'personal' users (Table 2: 48/146, 32.88%, of whom 31 were on Bilibili and 17 on TikTok), so the row pools the two platforms; the paper gives no platform-specific misinformation share. This is the ONLY falsity share in the paper: no overall misinformation rate for all 146 videos, and no rate for the professional uploader categories, is reported. breadth coded 'misleading' because the label covers oversimplification, which a partly-true video can attract. The source_quote is truncated to a contiguous span because the article text is two-column and the sentence's continuation ('were identified as containing misinformation') is interleaved with the other column; the full sentence is preserved in rob.item10_quote.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, deliberately: (1) the JAMA (median 2.00 overall, 1.00 Bilibili, 2.00 TikTok), modified DISCERN (3.00 everywhere), PEMAT intelligibility (70% vs 64%) and operability (67% on both) figures in Table 1. These are QUALITY instruments and, decisively, they are reported only as medians of a scale, not as a share of videos - the rule is that a scale reported only as a mean/median is not a share, so no row. The PEMAT '70%' and '67%' look like percentages but are percentages of criteria met within a video, not percentages of videos. (2) The theme counts n=8/4/6/10/6 in Section 3.7: these sum to 34 across 31 videos because a video could carry several themes, so they are not a partition and any share built on them would be a cross-category sum (barred by R8). (3) Structural distributions (uploader type, presentation format, content theme in Tables 2 and 4) are not falsity measures. (4) The Discussion's 'approximately half of the TikTok videos were misleading' refers to Yeung et al.'s ADHD study, i.e. a figure cited from elsewhere - excluded by R8. The one judgement call worth flagging: this is fundamentally a quality-appraisal paper, and had Section 3.7 not existed it would have been a QUALITY-only exclusion.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis; single-day census (25 February 2025) of the top 100 search hits for the Chinese keyword for Kawasaki disease on TikTok (Chinese version) and Bilibili, retrieved from newly registered accounts to suppress personalisation; 146 of 200 videos retained after excluding duplicates, adverts, off-topic and non-original videos (93 TikTok, 53 Bilibili). Two clinician raters scored every video independently (each video scored twice by rater 1 and once by rater 2), a third resolved disagreement; ICC 0.89 (JAMA), 0.72 (DISCERN), 0.85 (intelligibility), 0.83 (operability), intra-rater 0.96/0.76/0.80/0.84. No reliability statistic is given for the misinformation classification, which came from a qualitative Colaizzi thematic analysis applied only to the 48 individual-user videos. No sampling of non-searched or non-Chinese content; authors note the top-100 restriction as a limitation.
rob.item6_quote: Additionally, we conducted a systematic qualitative thematic analysis of videos uploaded by individual users that contained inaccurate information. Each individual video was allowed to be assigned to multiple themes.
rob.item10_quote: Overall, 64.58% (31/48) of videos uploaded by individual users were identified as containing misinformation.
